evaluation.positioning_hook: A hard-charging San Francisco doctor discovers a blood disease spreading through sex workers, then has to hunt the vampire lover who infected the woman she loves before the city’s elite cover it up.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate — a doctor, a lover, a vampire outbreak, and a citywide cover-up — which gives the script a clear genre audience. The reach is narrower than a mainstream horror title because the voice is highly specific and the sexual politics are front-and-center.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the opening pages: Dr. Diana Frost identifies a blood pathogen, then the script reveals it as vampirism tied to Marsha and the women in the ward. The engine is easy to explain in one breath, and the hospital-to-night-hunt progression is clean.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Frost has a strong physical and emotional profile — a muscular, sexually self-possessed doctor whose professional certainty gets wrecked by betrayal. Van Trapp and Rose give the story a workable triangle, though Frost is the clear center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script fuses medical procedural language, lesbian melodrama, and vampire mythology in a way that feels idiosyncratic rather than generic. The boldness is in the tonal mashup and the unapologetic erotic charge, even when the execution leans pulpy.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating from diagnosis to infection to confrontation to full supernatural siege, with set pieces that keep changing the battlefield. Some middle passages repeat the same emotional beat of jealousy and suspicion, but the final act drives hard.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A lesbian hospital administrator hunting a vampire lover through a foggy San Francisco underworld is a fresh enough combination to stick. The idea is instantly legible once it clicks, even though the underlying vampire framework is familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The hospital, the red-light district, the church, and the elite Van Trapp residence all carry distinct texture, and San Francisco is used as a moody container. The world is vivid in atmosphere, but it is not especially layered beyond the immediate hunt.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: This has a very particular register: lurid, erotic, melodramatic, and knowingly pulpy, with sudden bursts of gore and camp dialogue. The script knows exactly what kind of midnight movie it wants to be.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material around sexuality, betrayal, and institutional hypocrisy, but the script mostly plays those ideas on the surface. The emotional material is present, yet the piece is built to move rather than to accumulate subtext.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Frost/Rose/Van Trapp gives the film a workable triangle, and the supporting hospital staff add friction and social pressure. Still, the story is fundamentally powered by one lead and two key relationships rather than a true ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Diana Frost
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, mid-30s, lesbian, physician, physically imposing, emotionally guarded.
lead_characters.hook: A brilliant hospital doctor with a bodybuilder’s build and a tightly controlled emotional life, Diana Frost discovers the blood plague, then gets forced into a personal war when the infection reaches the woman she loves. She is clinically sharp, sexually confident, and increasingly feral under pressure, which makes her both the investigator and the story’s most volatile weapon.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Sigourney Weaver in Alien or Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs — a commanding, intelligent lead who has to project authority, vulnerability, and physical danger in the same role.

lead_characters.name: Rose
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s-30s, lesbian, Frost’s lover, married to John Donnely.
lead_characters.hook: Rose is the emotional fault line of the story: tender with Frost, conflicted about John, and increasingly vulnerable to Marsha’s seduction. She reads as wounded rather than passive, and the script uses her as the human cost of the infection and the betrayal at the center of the film.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the aching, morally complicated intimacy of Julianne Moore in The End of the Affair or Patricia Clarkson in High Art — desire, guilt, and emotional ambiguity all in one part.

lead_characters.name: Eldon Van Trapp
lead_characters.demographics: Man, middle-aged, hospital administrator, polished, closeted or sexually fluid, socially powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Van Trapp is the elegant institutional insider who starts as Frost’s ally and becomes her uneasy partner in the vampire hunt. He’s vain, witty, and morally compromised, but the script gives him a real arc from bureaucratic cynic to desperate believer.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charm turning to panic, like John Lithgow in Dexter or Ian McKellen in Gods and Monsters — a polished exterior cracking under supernatural pressure.

lead_characters.name: Marsha
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, adult, vampire, seductive, predatory, sexually dominant.
lead_characters.hook: Marsha is the story’s erotic antagonist: a vampiric high priestess who weaponizes desire, humiliation, and appetite. She is less a mystery than a force of nature, and the script leans into her as a glamorous, monstrous embodiment of temptation and contagion.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime Catherine Deneuve in The Hunger or Tilda Swinton in Only Lovers Left Alive energy — a role built around seduction, menace, and the pleasure of playing a predator who owns every room.

lead_characters.name: Eldon Van Trapp
lead_characters.demographics: Man, middle-aged, hospital administrator, polished, closeted or sexually fluid, socially powerful.
lead_characters.hook: Van Trapp is the elegant institutional insider who starts as Frost’s ally and becomes her uneasy partner in the vampire hunt. He’s vain, witty, and morally compromised, but the script gives him a real arc from bureaucratic cynic to desperate believer.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charm turning to panic, like John Lithgow in Dexter or Ian McKellen in Gods and Monsters — a polished exterior cracking under supernatural pressure.

lead_characters.name: John Donnely
lead_characters.demographics: Man, adult, Rose’s husband/ex-husband, emotionally wounded.
lead_characters.hook: John is the damaged heterosexual counterweight to the Frost/Rose relationship, and the script uses him to sharpen the betrayal and regret in Rose’s life. He’s not a villain so much as a reminder of the marriage and history Rose is trying to outgrow.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the bruised dignity of Billy Crudup in Jesus’ Son or Mark Ruffalo in You Can Count on Me — a man trying to stay composed while the emotional ground shifts under him.

lead_characters.name: Father Joseph Pina
lead_characters.hook: Father Pina is the brief but useful spiritual counterweight who gives Frost access to holy water and a moment of moral grounding. He’s warm, practical, and not written as a caricature, which helps the film pivot from lust to exorcism logic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact character role with the calm authority of Ed Harris in A History of Violence or Philip Seymour Hoffman in Doubt — a small part that lands because it carries moral weight.

lead_characters.name: Ali Cole
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, adult, talk-show host, media personality.
lead_characters.hook: Ali Cole is the public-facing voice of panic and curiosity, turning the outbreak into spectacle. She’s a useful pressure valve for exposition and a reminder that the disease has already become a civic story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp cameo-plus role in the vein of Jane Krakowski in 30 Rock or Parker Posey in Best in Show — a chance to play polished media absurdity with precision.

lead_characters.name: Simon Markstien
lead_characters.demographics: Man, adult, comedian, Jewish, talk-show guest.
lead_characters.hook: Simon is the comic interruption who accidentally names the truth before anyone else will say it. He’s brief, but he gives the script a sly public-relations beat and a little pressure-release humor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing comic turn that lets an actor do the fast, disruptive energy of Bob Einstein in Curb Your Enthusiasm — one joke, perfectly timed, that changes the room.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Parker
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, adult, patient, first known victim.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is the opening-case patient whose violent transformation announces the film’s rules. She’s not a character with a long arc, but she gives the outbreak its first body and its first shock.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a high-impact horror opening role, the kind that gives an actor the unforgettable first-act blast of Drew Barrymore in Scream — brief screen time, maximum imprint.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a physically imposing woman who can play authority, erotic confidence, and action intensity.
Supporting roles skew adult and character-specific, with one polished male administrator, one seductive female antagonist, and several hospital staff roles.

notable_requirements: Hospital ward, lab, office, apartment, church/cathedral, red-light district street, hotel/mission interior, car work, and a foggy San Francisco exterior palette.
Night exteriors are a major visual component.

technical.vfx_details: Practical and optical creature transformations, vampire morphs, smoke/ectoplasm effects, blood effects, and a few supernatural manifestations.
technical.sfx_needs: Heavy blood work, creature makeup, glass breakage, falls, impalement-style effects, and fire/smoke practicals.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best suited to a genre streamer, specialty distributor, or cult-midnight theatrical play.

budget.note: The film is contemporary and mostly interior, but the creature work, blood effects, night exteriors, and multiple vampire transformations will keep it above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: Diana Frost is a narrow lead ask: physically commanding, sexually credible, emotionally controlled, and able to carry both procedural authority and horror escalation.

development.note: The script’s pulpy erotic tone is a feature, but the buyer conversation will center on whether the camp, sexuality, and gore are being pitched as intentional style rather than tonal accident.

comp_set.title: The Hunger
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the erotic vampire lane, the glamorous predator energy, and the sense of urban nocturnal decadence.

comp_set.title: Near Dark
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the gritty, night-driven vampire hunt and the blend of romance, violence, and genre cool.

comp_set.title: The Lost Boys
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the pop-culture vampire energy and the accessible, high-style horror packaging.

comp_set.title: Jennifer's Body
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the sexualized horror register and the way desire and predation are fused into the monster logic.

comp_set.title: Only Lovers Left Alive
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the moody, sensual vampire atmosphere and the adult, character-first approach to the mythology.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult horror fans who like sexy, stylish, character-driven vampire movies with a cult edge.
audience_target.demographics: 18-49 skew, slightly female-leaning, genre-literate, streamer-friendly, midnight-movie audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, limited cast, and mostly practical creature work keep it in indie feature territory, though the night shoots and effects push it toward the upper end.

types_of_buyers: producer-directors looking for a stylish calling-card feature
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult vampire lane where style, sexuality, and a strong lead performance are the selling points. It is especially attractive to buyers who want a cult-friendly horror title with a clear poster image and a contained production footprint.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the story resolves its central infection and confrontation cleanly, and no secondary character is built as a clear franchise anchor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead role is a star-making engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Diana Frost is written as a rare horror protagonist who can carry authority, sexuality, and physical menace at once, which gives the project real casting leverage. That is the kind of part that attracts actor-forward buyers and performers looking for a signature genre turn.
strengths.evidence: The microscope opening, the weight-room scene, the beach confrontation, and the final gunfight all frame Frost as both clinician and predator.

strengths.what_it_means: The film has a clean commercial engine: a doctor discovers a blood plague, then learns it is vampirism tied to the woman her lover infected. That clarity helps the script travel quickly in a buyer meeting and makes the marketing hook easy to communicate.
strengths.evidence: The hospital ward of dying women, the Marsha reveal, and the Society of Vampirism card all sharpen the central reveal.

strengths.what_it_means: The script knows it is a lurid, erotic, midnight-movie horror piece, and that confidence is a commercial asset because it gives the project a defined lane instead of a generic vampire wrapper. Buyers who want cult identity will understand exactly what they are getting.
strengths.evidence: The sex-paper personals, the church/holy water sequence, the bat-creature transformation, and the neon-sign finale all lean into pulp spectacle.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The San Francisco setting adds mood without overcomplicating scope.
strengths.what_it_means: Foggy city streets, red-light districts, churches, and hospital interiors create a strong visual package that feels bigger than the budget. That helps the film look premium on a contained spend.
strengths.evidence: Broadway at night, the bay fog, the mission, and the hospital exteriors all recur as atmospheric anchors.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The relationship triangle gives the movie emotional traction.
strengths.what_it_means: Frost, Rose, and Van Trapp create a triangle of desire, betrayal, and reluctant alliance that can keep the audience engaged between set pieces. That gives the film more than just monster mechanics and makes it attractive to actors who want interpersonal heat.
strengths.evidence: The Frost/Rose apartment scenes, Donnely’s visit, and Van Trapp’s uneasy partnership with Frost all deepen the emotional stakes.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable horror package: a commanding female lead, a simple-to-pitch vampire outbreak engine, and a very specific erotic-cult tone. Because the story is contemporary, interior-heavy, and effects-driven rather than effects-dependent, it can play as a stylish indie genre buy with real poster appeal.

items.area: The tone leans hard into camp.
items.detail: The script’s dialogue and sexualized presentation are intentionally lurid, but that also narrows the buyer conversation to audiences who want a knowingly pulpy vampire movie. For some buyers, the question will be whether the camp is a feature or a liability.

items.area: The lead ask is unusually specific.
items.detail: Diana Frost needs a performer who can credibly play a physically imposing doctor, a lesbian romantic lead, and an action-horror protagonist without losing authority. That narrows casting more than the page may suggest.

items.area: The middle section repeats the same emotional pressure.
items.detail: A lot of the second act cycles through jealousy, betrayal, and suspicion between Frost, Rose, and Marsha before the supernatural siege fully takes over. That keeps the movie moving, but it also means the emotional escalation is more incremental than explosive.

items.area: The effects and night work will shape the spend.
items.detail: Creature transformations, blood-heavy attacks, glass breaks, smoke effects, and multiple night exteriors push this above a bare-bones indie. It is still producible, but the practical horror work is a real line item.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal and casting-related: this is a deliberately lurid camp-horror piece, and buyers will either lean into that identity or hesitate. The production is still manageable, but the lead role and the practical creature work are the two places where the package will be judged most closely.
